analytic.title: Real-Time Scheduling and Analysis of OpenMP Programs with Spin Locks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Locking protocol is an essential component in resource management of real-time systems, which coordinates mutually exclusive accesses to shared resources from different tasks. OpenMP is a promising framework for multi-core realtime embedded systems as well as provides spin locks to protect shared resources. In this paper, we propose a resource model for analyzing OpenMP programs with spin locks. Based on our resource model, we also develop a technique for analyzing the blocking time which impacts the total workload. Notably, the resource model provides detailed resource access behavior of the programs, making our blocking analysis more accurate. Further, we derive the schedulability analysis for real-time OpenMP tasks with spin locks protecting shared resources. Experiments with realistic OpenMP programs are conducted to evaluate the performance of our method.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time and embedded systems are being used widely in the modern society of today. In real-time systems, tasks might share resources in the system which can give rise to variations in response time of the tasks. Violating these timing constraints in such systems may lead to catastrophic consequences such as loss of human life. Therefore, realtime systems must manage resources in a way such that timing correctness can be guaranteed. Locking protocol is an essential component in resource management of real-time systems, which coordinates mutually exclusive accesses to shared physical/logical resources by different tasks.

Multi-cores are widespread in today's real-time systems for high performance and low power consumption. To fully utilize the computation power of multi-core processors, the software must be parallelized. OpenMP [1] is the de facto parallel programming framework which not only widely used in high-performance and general computing but also drawing increasing attention in the embedded and realtime computing domain [2]. Meanwhile, OpenMP framework provides fundamental locking protocols which are spin locks to protect shared resources. The workload structure of OpenMP programs is similar to real-time task graph models, and have been modeled as Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) task models.

There has been much work on scheduling and analysis of DAG task models generated by OpenMP programs [3]- [5]. However, a common limitation of existing techniques is that they all assume different tasks in the system are independent of each other in resource sharing, which is not usually employed in practice. In an OpenMP program, different regions of the program may compete for shared resources, such as shared peripheral devices or global data structures. To our best knowledge, [4] is the only work studied the spin locks in OpenMP programs. In [4], a technique has been developed for scheduling parallel real-time tasks with spin locks. Moreover, the blocking time contributing to the workload that may delay a task's finishing time is systematically defined and analyzed. They evaluate this method with realistic OpenMP programs. However, the blocking analysis in [4] use unspecific information, e.g., the number of resource accesses and the worst-case time of every access, which may lead to an overestimation of the blocking time. Also, the experiments in [4] conduct with the OpenMP workload using the measurement parameters of OpenMP programs, such as the execution time of every resource access. These parameters are measured while running the programs which are not guaranteed to be safe upper bounds of the desired parameters.

To avoid these pessimistic results, in this paper, we develop a new blocking time analysis technique for OpenMP programs with spin locks, where the resource access behavior is analyzed in a detailed manner. We safely bounded the OpenMP program parameters by Chronos [6], which is a comprehensive static analysis covering all the hardware and software behaviors. We transform OpenMP programs into DAG task models. Moreover, we also propose a resource model using control flow graphs (CFG). This model gives the exact worst-case duration of each access and information about which resource is accessed by which part of the task. Based on the resource model, we then develop a technique for blocking analysis, which makes the result of blocking time more precise. Further, we derive the schedulability analysis for OpenMP tasks with spin locks. To our best knowledge, we are the first to work on modeling resource access behavior in a detailed manner based on realistic parallel programs. We conduct experiments to evaluate the precision improvement compared with [4] using workload generated according to OpenMP programs. The experimental results show that our approach outperforms [4] under different settings.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: In this section, we introduce concepts and notations related to the OpenMP program, which will be used in the rest of this paper. Furthermore, we give an example of an OpenMP program transforming into a DAG task model.

Loop parallelization is one of the most critical parallelism strategies in applications which can reduce considerable cache misses [7]. The fundamental loop parallelizing methods in OpenMP is parallel loop construct which takes a parallel for directive for supporting parallelism. Meanwhile, OpenMP framework provides critical and atomic construct to protect shared resources. The detailed descriptions of OpenMP constructs are as followed.

• parallel loop construct: parallel loop construct takes a directive-based approach for supporting parallelism. An OpenMP program starts with a parallel for directive, which constructs the associated parallel loop region including all the code enclosed in an area following the parallel for directive. By applying it to proper loops, programs can be parallelized efficiently.

Besides, for maintaining the correctness of a program, the programmer must choose appropriate loops to parallelize. • critical construct: critical construct restricts execution of the associated structured block to a single thread at a time. An optional name may be used to identify the critical construct. All critical constructs without a name are considered to have the same unspecified name. div.head: III. MODELS
div.p: In this section, we give formal models, including task model, resource model and scheduling model. These models are inspired by the semantics of OpenMP programs.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: A task τ i has a period T i , a relative deadline D i and a workload structure modeled by A task τ i Directed Acyclic Graph D(τ i ) = V i , E i with vertex and edge labels. Tasks have constrained deadlines, i.e., D i ≤ T i . The vertices
div.formula: {v 1 i , • • • , v n i } of D(τ i ) represents the different vertices in D(τ i ), where n is the number of vertices in D(τ i ). Each vertex v u i is labeled c(v u i )
div.p: , which is the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the corresponding vertex. We use C i to denote the total WCET of all vertices of τ i and
div.formula: C i = n u=1 c(v u i )
div.p: . The utilization of task τ i is U i = C i /T i and the density of task τ i is γ i = C i /D i . In this paper, we only consider DAG tasks with γ i > 1, as those with γ i ≤ 1 can be executed sequentially and handled by existing techniques for sequential real time tasks.

Each edge (v u i , v v i ) of D(τ i ) represents the precedence relation between vertices v u i and v v i , where v u i is a predecessor of v v i , and v v i is a successor of v u i . We assume each DAG has a unique head vertex (with no predecessors) and a unique tail vertex (with no successors). This assumption does not limit the expressiveness of our model since one can always add a dummy head/tail vertex to a DAG having multiple entry/exit points. A complete path in a DAG task τ i is a sequence of
div.formula: vertices π = {v 1 i , v 2 i , • • • , v p i },
div.p: where the first element v 1 i is the head vertex of D(τ i ), and the last element v p i is the tail vertex of D(τ i ), and v j i is is a predecessor of v j+1 i in π i . The length of each path π is len(π) = v u i ∈π c(v u i ). We use L i to denote the longest length among all paths in D(τ i ): L i = max π∈D(τi) {len(π)}. Task τ i generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, which inherit τ i 's DAG workload structure D(τ i ). Let J be a job released by τ i , then we use r(J) to denote J's release time and f (J) to denote its finish time. The absolute deadline of J is calculated by r(J + D i ). At runtime, we say a vertex (of a job J) is eligible at some time point if all its predecessors (of the same job J) have been finished and thus it can immediately execute if there are available processors.

div.head: B. Resource Model
div.p: There is a limited set Q of n r serially-reusable shared resources Q = {l 1 , • • • , l nr } in the system, such as I/O ports, network links, message buffers, or other shared data structures. Spin locks protect resources, i.e., the program must acquire, hold and release the lock affiliated to l q before, during, and after executing the code segment accessing l q . We assume the code segment wrapped by a pair of lock acquisition and lock release does not cross different vertices. When a vertex v u i access to l q which is held by other vertices, v u i must spin non-preemptively until it successfully accesses l q . A vertex may access different shared resources and thus hold different locks. We simply assume that vertices request and hold at most one resource at a time. We use Q i denote the set of resources accessed by task τ i .
We make use of the control flow graph (CFG) of a task τ i for modeling its resource access behavior. The CFG G(τ i ) of task
div.formula: τ i consist of the CFG G(v u i ) of each vertex. Given a vertex v u i in task τ i , its CFG is a di- rected graph G(v u i ) = B u i , E u i . B u i = {b 1 u , b 2 u , • • • , b N u } is the set of the basic blocks in v u i . And E u i = {(b a u , b b u )|b b u is directly control dependent on b a u } is the set of control flow edges. Each basic block b x
div.p: u has a worst-case execution-time e(b x u ). Figure 2 is the control flow graph of the OpenMP task graph in Figure 1.

div.head: C. Scheduling Model
div.p: OpenMP tasks have been divided into two categories: tied and untied tasks [10]. A tied task, once started execution on one thread, can not migrate to another. In contrast, an untied task can be executed on different threads. In this paper, we consider untied tasks, since timing analysis for tied tasks has inherent complexity that would lead to unacceptably pessimistic response-time bounds [10].

There are in total m processors in the system, which can be partitioned into several subsets and each subset is assigned to a task. We use m i to denote the number of processors assigned to task τ i . At runtime, τ i is scheduled by a work-conserving scheduling algorithm [11] exclusively on these m i processors. Note that although a task τ i executes exclusively on its own m i processors, its timing behavior is still interfered by other tasks due to the contention on the shared resources. The response time R(J) of a job J is R(J) = f (J)r(J), and the worst-case response time
div.formula: (WCRT) R i of task τ i is the maximum R(J) among all its released jobs J. Task τ i is schedulable if R i ≤ D i .
div.p: The problem to solve is how to partition the m processors to each task such that it is guaranteed to be schedulable.

div.p: In this section, we first analyze the resource access behavior based on the resource model above. Next, we give an approach to compute the maximum time of task access to a resource.

div.p: For a path π i in τ i , it can be redefined as a weighted digraph G q (π i ) which is a sub-graph of G q (τ i ). Our analysis uses the concept of demand bound function (dbf ) [12], which is an established framework in schedulability theory. Intuitively, a dbf expresses the accumulated execution time that a task set can demand from the processor within any time interval of a given length. In our analysis, we consider the accumulated time of l q can be accessed by a path π i in τ i from the processors within any time interval of a given length. We use Π i denote the all paths in D(τ i ) where Π i = {π 1 , π 2 , . . . , π n }. Note that each path in Π i does not contain the same vertex. div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULT
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the performance of our approach in terms of acceptance ratio with the workload generated by OpenMP programs, in comparison with the approach in [4]. Acceptance ratio is a ratio between the number of task sets that are schedulable and the number of the whole task sets.

Algorithm 2 Algorithm of schedulability test. We select seven programs from WCET Benchmarks suit [16]. Table I shows the program name, a brief description, as well as comments of programs. These benchmarks used in our evaluation explore different program structures and memory access patterns include nested loops, nonrectangular loop nests, row/column-based matrix accesses. To evaluate the same resources shared by different programs, we slightly modify the benchmarks by adding some codes. And we use OpenMP parallel loop construct for parallelization. We considered 12 types of resources, where the first 4 are shared data objects in the operating kernel accessed via system calls (i.e., time) or library calls (i.e., fprintf, printf, malloc). The remaining 8 are shared data structures or non-reusable routines protected by critical or atomic construct. Furthermore, we transform them into DAG models. Meanwhile, we modify Chronos [6] to analyze the program, calculate the execution times of its basic blocks, and construct its CFG. Chronos is built on top of the SimpleScalar simulator infrastructure, which allows the user to model a variety of processor platforms in software. We assume the programs are executed on m processors with shared memory. The architecture of each processor is with a 5-stage pipeline, in-order execution, and separate L1 instruction and data caches. Both instruction and data caches have cache size 2 KB, block size 32 B, cache associativity 2, and perfect LRU replacement policy.

For each task set, we pick n programs in Table I. The deadline D i of each task is generated in a similar way Figure 8. The experimental result compare with [4] with [4]: after L i is fixed, D i is generated according to a normalized ratio R n between L i and D i . The period T i is set to be equal to D i . Notably, both our work and [4] are based on the classic Graham's bound [17]. Thus if there are no resource access contentions, the schedulability of our result and [4] are the same. Thus, the gap of the performance between our results and [4] is because of the blocking time generated by shared resource accesses. In Figure 8 (a)-(d), we set a basic configuration, and in each group of experiments, vary one parameter while keeping others unchanged. The basic configuration is as follows: n = 3, R n = 0.150, the number of resource types is 12.

Figure 8 shows the experimental result. We compare our approach with the approach for unordered spin locks in [4]. The dashed red line represents our test result, while the solid blue line represents the test result of [4]. In Figure 8 (a) and (b), the processor number is set to be m = 8 as well as the processor number is m = 32 in Figure 8 (c) and (d). Figure 8 (a) shows the schedulability of two methods under different task n. We can observe that the acceptance ratios of both tests decrease as the number of tasks increases. Nevertheless, our method decreases at a slower rate. In Figure 8 (b), we show the schedulability of two methods under different normalized ratio R n . The acceptance ratios of both tests decrease when the normalized ratio increased. This is because using our task generation method, relatively deadlines and periods become shorter when the normalized ratio increased. And these tasks have a low tolerance for blocking time caused by other tasks. In Figure 8 (c) and (d), the results have the same trend as in Figure (a) and(c). However, we can observe all the acceptance ratios increases in comparison with (a) and (b). This is because the increase in the number of processors makes the longest path shorter under the parallel loop parallelization method. In Figure (c), the acceptance ratios of both tests decrease at a slower rate as the number of tasks increases comparing with (a). At the point of task number n = 5, we can observe that both method's acceptance ratios are around 20 percent with m = 32, while the acceptance ratios of both methods are close to zero with m = 8. In Figure (d), we can observe that the acceptance ratios of our approach increase more comparing with [4]. Especially, at the point of R n = 0.250, the acceptance ratio of our method is over 30 percent, while the acceptance rate of [4] is close to zero. From the above results, our approach consistently outperforms the state-ofthe-art in [4] under different parameter settings.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: OpenMP Tasks Analysis: Vargas et al. [18], for the first time, modeled OpenMP task systems by DAGs. Serrano et al. [10] first developed the worst-case response time (WCRT) bound analysis for the OpenMP DAG task model, which distinguishes two types of OpenMP tasks: tied and untied tasks. Moreover, Sun et al. [19] have shown that the tied task has extremely bad timing behavior with the current OpenMP compliant scheduling algorithms. Jiang et al. [4] discuss the average-case performance analysis of OpenMP programs, which is significantly different from the worstcase response time analysis in this paper. The measurementbased approaches used in [4] without modeling the structures of the tasks explicitly. In contrast, the blocking time analysis in this paper explicitly models the structure and timing properties of OpenMP programs, which formally derives valuable timing boundaries based on that information.

Locking Protocols: Resource sharing problems have been studied in plentiful literature for periodic and sporadic task systems. Some work exists to address this problem in graph-based real-time task models, such as the DRT task model [12] and generalized multiframe (GMF) task model [20]. Zhuo [21] consider extending the existing protocols to graph-based task models under static priority schedulers, in which blocking times are represented by blocking functions. Based on the DRT task model, Guan et al. [22] develop a protocol called ACP to deal with branching structures in the context of EDF scheduling. Besides, the locking protocols also have been studied with other parallel graphbased models. These models have multiple edges going out a vertex with forking semantics instead of conditional branching semantics. For instance, S. Dinh et al. [23] focus on analyzing blocking time in parallel systems with shared resources. They provide a schedulability test for federated scheduling protected by spin locks. [4] considers locks for parallel real-time task model, which adopts the federated scheduling framework with spin locks. As we mentioned before, [4] analyzes the impact of the blocking time to the total workload and the longest path length jointly. However, they use abstract shared resources for blocking analysis, which leads to pessimism in analysis precision. The contribution of this paper is to address this pessimism by modeling a detailed resource model.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Motivated by OpenMP, many DAG models have been proposed and analyzed. However, few of them consider the OpenMP task's shared resources problems. In this paper, we make efforts on scheduling and analyzing OpenMP tasks with spin locks. In particular, we model the resource access behavior and analyze the blocking time for computing the worst-case response-time bounds. Experiments with both realistic OpenMP programs show the effectiveness of our proposed analysis techniques. As future work, we will investigate OpenMP programs with priority-ordered and FIFOordered spin locks.
